extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students working in analytic geometry, classical mechanics, and celestial perturbation theory
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and criteria for recognising and reducing a general second‑order surface equation to a primitive form (ellipsoid, hyperboloid, cone, paraboloid, cylinders, planes), together with related methods (surface of revolution test, principal planes/axes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive forms of second-order surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: A surface of the second order is represented by a general second-order equation in three variables which, when reduced, takes one of a set of primitive forms enumerated (ellipsoid, hyperboloid of one sheet, cone, hyperboloid of two sheets, elliptic cylinder, straight line, hyperbolic cylinder, two planes, two parallel planes, single plane, elliptic paraboloid, hyperbolic paraboloid, parabolic cylinder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper lists primitive forms (labelled (1)–(8)) and associates ranges of the parameter a (positive/negative/zero) with each species. Example: 'a > 0 an ellipsoid', 'a > 0 hyperboloid of one sheet', '@ = 0 a cone', etc. Use the sign and value of the canonical coefficient(s) after reduction to decide the species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction method by completing squares
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the general second-order equation f(x,y,z)=0 as x^2 + P x + Q = 0 where P is linear in y,z and Q is quadratic; complete the square in x, then in the resulting quadratic in y and z, iterating until the primitive form is reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise: (1) arrange as a^2 + P a + Q = 0; (2) complete the square in a to get (a + 1/2 P)^2 + (Q - 1/4 P^2)=0; (3) write the remainder as K y^2 + Ly + M and complete the square in y, then in z. The process terminates earlier in special cases (see 'excepted cases'). The method yields the primitive form (one of the enumerated types) and identifies conjugate/diametral planes and the centre when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of exceptional cases (missing squared terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: When some squared terms are missing (deficient equation), the general completing-square process must be modified: add and subtract an auxiliary term, choose a parameter to form complete squares, or otherwise rearrange to one of the primitive forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: if all squares are absent, add and subtract βx^2 and choose β so that the residual becomes a square; determine β from the condition that a certain quadratic in the remaining variables becomes a perfect square. The examples show how to obtain primitive forms (2), (3), etc., even in deficient cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for a surface of revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: A second-order surface is a surface of revolution iff there exists a scalar k such that, when k(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) is added to the quadratic part, the result is a positive complete square (i.e., the quadratic form becomes a perfect square).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationally: add k(a^2 + y^2 + z^2) to the terms of second order and attempt to make the whole expression equal to a complete square; if such k exists (solve the resulting cubic for k), the surface is one of revolution and the axis/centre follow from the completed-square form. If no such k exists, the surface is not of revolution. The paper gives worked examples and notes that the determining equation for k is cubic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding cyclic (principal) planes and axes via sum/difference of squares
rubrics_metrics.description: When the surface is not a surface of revolution, one can always choose a scalar λ so that the quadratic form becomes equivalent to the sum or difference of two squares; the final equation for λ is a cubic, whose roots yield cyclic planes and principal axes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method reduces the quadratic part to two squares (or sum/difference), from which cyclic planes and principal axes can be read off. The cubic for λ provides the directions; the paper outlines using this to determine principal planes and axes without forming the cubic for semi-axes directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical examples to identify surface species
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the completing-square reduction and exceptional-case manipulations to concrete polynomial examples to determine whether the surface is an hyperboloid (one or two sheets), elliptic cylinder, cone, hyperbolic paraboloid, elliptic paraboloid, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article includes multiple worked examples showing algebraic rearrangement, identification of centre and conjugate planes, and final recognition of the primitive form. Use the same algebraic rearrangements and checks on constants/coefficients in new cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for whether a given quadratic equation represents a cone
rubrics_metrics.description: A second-order equation equivalent to one of the primitive forms with the scalar parameter equal to zero corresponds to a cone; identification arises when, after completing squares, the constant term drops out producing homogeneous quadratic equal to zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In examples, after completing squares and appropriate sign changes, if the resulting form matches a primitive cone form and the constant term is zero (or can be removed by appropriate operations), classify as a cone and determine its axis from the linear factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radius of circumscribing sphere of a tetrahedron (formulaic relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a tetrahedron, let the products (rectangles) of pairs of opposite edges be denoted (notation in text), let S be half their sum, and V the volume; then the radius R of the circumscribing sphere is expressible by a symmetric formula in those edge-rectangle quantities and V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper derives an explicit algebraic formula relating R to the products of opposite edges and the volume V (presented in the original as a factorised root of three expressions). Use the relationships among opposite-edge products, dihedral angles, and volume to compute R. (Note: the printed formula is given in the paper in the context of preceding algebraic reductions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition IV — area of opposite face from a solid angle and its containing edges
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a solid angle at a tetrahedron vertex and the three edges from that vertex (with included dihedral angles), there is an expression for the area of the opposite face in terms of the squares of those edges and the cosines of the dihedral angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives squared-length relations (e.g., a^2 + f^2 − 2df cos β, etc.) and substitutes these into a four-term expression, ultimately producing A^2 expressed as a sum of squared areas and cross terms: A2 = A1^2 + A2^2 + A3^2 − 2A1A2 cos(d) − 2A1A3 cos(e) − 2A2A3 cos(f). When one dihedral is right angle the formula simplifies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition V — distances from a vertex to incenter and excenters of opposite face
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions are provided for the distances from a tetrahedron vertex to the incenter and the excenters of the opposite triangular face in terms of the side lengths and area of that face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The derivations substitute cosine formulas from earlier propositions and reduce to explicit algebraic expressions (the paper shows long reductions). The formulas include symmetrical rational expressions in squared sides and twice-area terms; analogous expressions are given for distances to the circumcenter and others (e.g., d_y' = 16 A_1^2, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition VI — sum of squares identity for triangle centres in space
rubrics_metrics.description: For a plane triangle considered in space, the sum of the squares of the distances of the inscribed and escribed circle centres from a point equals four times the square of the distance of the circumcentre plus twelve times the square of its radius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper shows adding values of d_i^2 obtained earlier yields: d1^2 + d2^2 + d3^2 + d4^2 = 4(d_circum^2 + R^2) + 2 R1 R2 terms (reduced to the simpler identity). In the special case where d_circum = 0, one gets p + dp + df + dz = 12 R^2 (a known relation). Use previously derived expressions for individual d_i^2 and algebraic summation to verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of osculating (variable) elements for a disturbed planet
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the eccentric anomaly w and relations m − e sin w = n t + e − w, r = a(1 − e cos w) to derive time-variations of mean motion and orbital elements under perturbing forces represented by a function R (depending on distances only). The osculating elements are made to vary so that the instantaneous orbit has first-order contact with the true perturbed trajectory (6R = 0 condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key steps: derive differential relations for elements by taking variations while enforcing the contact conditions (δR = 0), neglect second-order infinitesimals from impulses perpendicular to the orbital plane, write R as function of orbital longitude and inclination variables, and obtain differential equations for a, e, i, Ω, ω, etc. The paper presents explicit differential formulae and demonstrates elimination/substitution to reach Lagrange-like planetary equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: General formula in finite differences by separation of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: A method is given to derive finite-difference formulae (e.g., Σ(u_z v_x) and higher-order analogues) by separating operation symbols and manipulating them algebraically (introducing an operator symbol @ and its powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat operators symbolically: introduce @ transforming sequences, raise symbols to powers, substitute expansions (e.g., (1 + A.B + ...) analogues) and expand to obtain general finite difference identities. The technique provides alternative derivations to those based on generating functions and yields Condorcet-like expressions for certain sums; examples and expansions are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric criterion for common tangents to two circles
rubrics_metrics.description: If DD' is a common tangent to two circles with centres A and B and meets the line joining centres at C (or C'), then proportions AD:BD' :: AC:BC (or AD + BD' :: AC' : BC') determine the points where tangents meet the line of centres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two cases: tangents on same side of AB leads to AD:BD' :: AC:BC; tangent passing between circles (radii on opposite sides) gives AD + BD' :: AC':BC'. Use parallelism of radii perpendicular to the tangent and simple Euclidean proportion to find the intersection points; the paper derives further product relations when circles intersect.
